12834: The word puritan carries two meanings — one historical and specific, the other general and everyday. Both come from the same root idea: the desire to be pure. Understanding both will give you the full picture.

In the 1500s and 1600s, England had an official church called the Church of England. A group of people believed this church was still too similar to the Roman Catholic Church — too full of rituals, ceremonies, bishops in fancy robes, and traditions they considered corrupt or unnecessary. They wanted to purify the church — to strip it down to what they believed was simple, honest, Bible-based Christianity.

These people were called Puritans.

They were deeply serious about religion. They believed every moment of life should be dedicated to God. They rejected things like elaborate church decorations, theatrical performances, gambling, and excessive celebration. They held the Bible as the absolute authority on how to live. They were not just religious on Sundays — their faith controlled every single part of their daily life.

Many Puritans were persecuted in England for their beliefs. A famous group of them sailed to America in 1620 on the Mayflower — these are the people often called the Pilgrims. They founded colonies in New England and shaped much of early American culture. Their influence on American values around hard work, self-discipline, and moral seriousness is still visible today.

So when written with a capital P, Puritan refers to this specific, real, historical group of people.

Over time, the word left its historical box and entered everyday language with a lowercase p. Now it is used to describe any person — in any time period, any country, any culture — who:

  • holds extremely strict moral or religious standards
  • is deeply uncomfortable with pleasure, fun, or anything they consider sinful or indulgent
  • tends to judge or disapprove of others who don't share those same strict standards
  • believes life should be disciplined, serious, and self-restrained

This person doesn't have to be religious. A puritan in the modern sense could be someone who is fanatically strict about healthy eating and looks down on anyone who eats junk food. Or someone who thinks any form of entertainment is a waste of time. Or someone who is deeply critical of any behaviour that doesn't meet their personal moral code.

The key idea is excessive strictness — especially when that strictness is imposed on or directed at others.
The Core Difference Between the Two Meanings

Puritan (capital P)puritan (lowercase p)
Who?A real, specific historical groupAny person, any era
When?1500s–1600s England and AmericaUsed any time, even today
Tone?Neutral / historical factOften slightly critical or negative

When you see a capital P, you are reading about history. When you see a lowercase p, you are reading a description of someone's personality or attitude — and it usually carries a slightly negative or critical tone, suggesting the person is too rigid, too judgmental, or takes the fun out of things.
How It Feels to Call Someone a Puritan Today

Calling someone a puritan today is almost never a compliment. It suggests they are:

  • Joyless — unable or unwilling to enjoy life's simple pleasures
  • Judgmental — quick to look down on others who live differently
  • Rigid — unable to bend or be flexible about rules and morals
  • Killjoys — the type of person who makes others feel guilty for having fun

For example: "He refused to come to the party and spent the whole evening lecturing us about alcohol — he's such a puritan."

Not everyone who is disciplined or morally serious is a puritan. The word specifically implies a kind of excessive or harsh strictness — often with a self-righteous edge, meaning the person not only follows strict rules themselves but also feels entitled to push those rules on others or criticise those who don't follow them.

A monk who quietly lives a disciplined life without judging others is not what people typically mean by a puritan. The word is best used when the strictness comes with disapproval of others.

Historically, a Puritan was a 16th–17th century English Protestant who wanted to purify the Church of England and lived by extremely strict religious and moral rules. In everyday modern use, a puritan is any person who holds very strict moral standards and tends to disapprove of pleasure, fun, or the lifestyle of those who don't share their rigid views.
12835:
Purlieu is a noun with a beautifully layered meaning. All its senses orbit one central idea: a borderland — a place at the edge of something larger, or a space that someone regularly inhabits as their own.

Here are its meanings, from the most concrete to the most abstract.
Meaning 1: The outskirts or surrounding area of a place

The most common meaning of purlieu is the area immediately surrounding a place — its fringes, edges, or outskirts. Think of it as the zone just outside the main thing, but still closely tied to it.

  • "She lived in the purlieus of the city, far from the busy center."
  • "The café was tucked away in the purlieus of the old cathedral."

Notice that it's often used in the plural (purlieus) when describing the surrounding area of a place. The singular purlieu works too, but the plural is especially natural in this sense.
Meaning 2: A person's regular haunt or familiar territory

Purlieu can also describe a place someone frequently visits or considers their own well-known ground — a personal domain, a stomping ground.

  • "The old library was his purlieu; he was there every single morning."
  • "She felt completely at ease here — this was her purlieu."

Here, the word carries a warm, possessive quality. It's not just a place — it's your place. The territory you know well and return to habitually.
Meaning 3: The scope or limits of something (abstract)

More abstractly, purlieu can refer to the range, sphere, or area of authority of something — what it covers or has jurisdiction over.

  • "This question falls entirely outside the purlieu of our department."
  • "Art and science overlap, but each has its own purlieu."

In this sense, it works similarly to words like domain, scope, province, or realm.
The historical sense (essential for reading older texts)

If you read older British literature or legal writing, you may encounter purlieu in a precise historical sense: a strip of land on the border of a royal forest — land that had once been part of the forest but was later separated from it, while still being partly subject to certain forest laws. The owner of purlieu land had special rights within it, but within constraints. It was neither fully forest nor fully free land. A true borderland.

You don't need this for everyday use, but understanding it clarifies why the word always carries that sense of an edge, a threshold, something between two larger things.

Whether it's the outskirts of a city, someone's habitual haunt, or the abstract limits of a subject, purlieu always describes something at the boundary or periphery of something larger — or a space that is claimed, familiar, and regularly returned to.
How it differs from similar words

Outskirts is simpler and more literal — just the edge of a city or town. Purlieu is more sophisticated and flexible, and can be used outside purely physical contexts.

Vicinity simply means "nearby area." Purlieu is richer — it suggests a defined surrounding zone with its own character, not just proximity.

Domain usually implies clear ownership or authority. Purlieu is looser — it's more about familiarity and regular presence than formal ownership.

Haunt (as a noun) means a place you frequently visit. Purlieu can carry this meaning too, but is more formal and literary in tone.
When you'll encounter it, and when to use it yourself

Purlieu is a literary and formal word. You won't hear it in casual conversation. You're most likely to encounter it in British literature (especially from the 19th and early 20th centuries), formal academic writing, or journalism with a literary lean.

You can use it yourself when describing the surrounding area of a place, someone's habitual territory, or the limits of something — and you want to do so with precision and an elevated, literary quality.
12836: To purloin something means to steal it, but in a quiet, sneaky, sly way — without force, without confrontation, and often without the victim noticing right away. Think of a pickpocket silently lifting a wallet, not a robber demanding it at gunpoint. The theft is secretive, smooth, and crafty.
What Makes It Different from Just "Steal"

"Steal" is a broad, everyday word. You can steal loudly, violently, impulsively, or calculatedly — the word doesn't judge how.

"Purloin" is more specific. It carries the idea of cunning and stealth. When someone purloins something, they:

  • Take it without drawing attention
  • Often rely on cleverness or opportunity, not force
  • Leave the victim unaware, at least for a while

So every act of purloining is an act of stealing, but not every act of stealing is purloining. A mugger who snatches a bag violently is stealing. A clever spy who slips a confidential document from a desk and replaces it with a copy is purloining.

Purloin has a slightly old-fashioned, formal, and literary quality. You will encounter it far more in books, legal writing, or formal speech than in everyday conversation. Because of this slightly elevated tone, the word is sometimes used with a touch of irony or humor — for example, describing someone sneaking a biscuit from a tin in the same sophisticated language you'd use for a master heist. That contrast creates a gentle comic effect.

It is never used to describe violent theft. It would sound wrong, even absurd, to say someone "purloined" a car by smashing a window and speeding away. The word belongs to the world of quiet, crafty, discreet taking.

Almost anything — but the word is especially well-suited to:

  • Small or portable objects — a key, a letter, a document, a ring, a pen
  • Information or ideas — a secret, a formula, a plan
  • Things of value that can be taken without a struggle — jewelry, money, rare items

The most famous literary use of this word is Edgar Allan Poe's story The Purloined Letter, in which a letter is stolen not by breaking into a safe, but by hiding it in plain sight — a perfect example of the quiet cleverness the word implies.

Purloin sits in an interesting middle ground. It is not a trivial or playful word — it does mean to steal, which is a serious act. However, because of its old-fashioned literary flavor, it is often used for:

  • Petty or small-scale theft (purloining a pen, purloining a slice of cake)
  • Elegant or sophisticated theft (a spy purloining state secrets)

It is almost never used for large-scale, brutal, or violent crimes. You would not say someone "purloined" a bank by threatening people with weapons.

• Someone had purloined the last slice of cake before I got to the kitchen.
  • The student purloined answers from his neighbor's exam paper.
  • Over the years, the dishonest clerk had purloined small amounts of cash from the register.
  • The enemy agent purloined the blueprints from the general's briefcase while he slept.
  • He had a habit of purloining phrases from other writers and presenting them as his own.
One-Line Summary to Remember It By
To purloin = to steal quietly, cleverly, and without confrontation — the word of a pickpocket, a spy, or a sly opportunist, never a brute.
12837:
Purport means the main meaning, substance, or overall message that something conveys — especially a document, statement, letter, or speech.

When you ask "what is the purport of this?" you are essentially asking: "What is this really saying? What is its overall substance and meaning?"

Think of it as the essential meaning that something carries within it — what a piece of writing or speech amounts to, in terms of its central message.
The Subtle But Important Shade of Meaning

Here is where purport becomes interesting and slightly different from simply saying "meaning."

The word often carries a quiet suggestion of "what something claims or appears to mean" — sometimes without you necessarily confirming that it is true, accurate, or fully genuine.

In other words, when you use "purport," you are sometimes reporting the meaning of something at a slight distance — you are saying "this is what it conveys or professes to convey," not necessarily "this is the truth."

This is a delicate but real nuance. It is why lawyers, scholars, and formal writers love this word — it lets them describe what a document says without fully endorsing it.

Imagine your friend hands you a very long, confusing legal letter and asks, "What does it say?"

You would not read every word aloud. Instead, you would say something like: "The overall purport of this letter is that they want you to vacate the apartment by the end of the month."

You are capturing the substance and core message of the letter — not quoting it, not summarising every detail, but conveying what it amounts to in meaning.

These examples move from simple to more nuanced, so you can see the word doing different kinds of work.

  • "She didn't understand the full purport of his words until the next morning."

Here, purport simply means the full meaning and significance of what he said — she didn't grasp it right away.

  • "The purport of the announcement was that the company would be laying off hundreds of workers."

Here, purport means the overall substance and message of the announcement.

  • "He conveyed the purport of the agreement to those who hadn't read it."

Here, he is communicating what the agreement amounts to — its essential meaning — to people who hadn't read it themselves.

  • "The purport of the document is unclear, and the court cannot act on it."

Here, a lawyer or judge is saying that the essential meaning and substance of the document is not clear enough to interpret.

  • "I understand the purport of what you are saying, even if I disagree with it."

Here, purport means the general meaning and thrust of someone's argument. The speaker grasps what the other person is driving at.
How Purport Differs From Similar Words

Since you want complete clarity, here is how purport sits among words that seem close to it:

Purport vs. Meaning
"Meaning" is a broad, everyday word. "Purport" is more formal and specific — it usually refers to the meaning of a communication as a whole (a document, a speech, a message), not just a single word or phrase. You would say the meaning of the word "liberty," but the purport of the letter.

Purport vs. Gist
"Gist" is informal and conversational — "give me the gist of it." Purport is formal and carries more weight. Gist just means a quick summary. Purport implies the substantive, essential meaning — what the thing actually amounts to and conveys.

Purport vs. Substance
These are very close. "Substance" focuses on the real content and material of something. "Purport" focuses on the meaning that it conveys — what it is saying or claiming to say. Purport has slightly more of a communicative and interpretive flavour.

Purport vs. Intent / Purpose
"Intent" and "purpose" are about what someone wanted to achieve — the goal behind something. Purport is about what something means or says, not why someone said it. A document can have a confusing purport but a clear intent, or vice versa.

"Purport" as a noun is a formal word. You will encounter it in legal writing, academic texts, journalism, formal letters, and serious literary prose. It would sound unusual in casual conversation — you would not typically say "what's the purport of your text message?" In everyday speech, people say "meaning," "gist," or "point" instead.

However, when you encounter it in reading, or when you need precision in formal writing, purport is exactly the right word when you want to describe the overall meaning and substance that something conveys or professes to convey.

If you can always remember this, you have truly learned the word:

Purport is the essential meaning and substance that a piece of communication conveys — often with a quiet suggestion that this is what it claims or appears to mean, without necessarily confirming it as true.
12838:
To purport means to claim or appear to be something — but with a built-in hint of doubt about whether that claim is actually true.

When you say something purports to be X, you are saying: "It is presenting itself as X, but I'm not fully convinced — or at least, I'm not vouching for it."

That small cloud of doubt is the soul of this word. Without it, you would just use "is."
Breaking It Down with a Simple Example

Imagine someone hands you a document and says it's a letter signed by the President.

  • If you believe it completely, you say: "This is a letter from the President."
  • If you're not sure — if you're just reporting what the document claims to be — you say: "This letter purports to be from the President."

That second sentence doesn't call the document a fake. It doesn't confirm it's real either. It simply reports the document's own claim while keeping your personal judgment neutral or skeptical. That's exactly what "purport" does — it creates a careful distance between what something says it is and what it actually is.

The verb almost always follows one of these two patterns:

Pattern 1: Something purports to be something.

"The painting purports to be an original Picasso."
"He purports to be a licensed doctor."

Pattern 2: Something purports to do something.

"This pill purports to cure insomnia in three days."
"The report purports to prove that the company was innocent."

Notice that the subject (the thing doing the "purporting") is usually not a person making a loud, active declaration. It's a thing — a document, a product, a piece of evidence, a person's identity — that is simply presenting itself in a certain way. The claim is quieter, more of an appearance than a shout.

You will also frequently see "purport" used in the passive voice:

"He is purported to be one of the richest men in the country."
"The artifact is purported to date back to ancient Egypt."

Here, the meaning shifts slightly toward "it is widely said or believed that…" — like a rumor or general reputation that the speaker doesn't personally confirm. It's still skeptical, but in a softer, more social way: "People say this, but don't hold me to it."
Why the Doubt Is Always There

This is the most important thing to understand: you would never use "purport" when you fully believe the claim.

Compare these two sentences:

❌ "Water purports to be made of hydrogen and oxygen."

That sounds wrong because water is made of hydrogen and oxygen — it's established fact. There's no room for doubt, so "purport" doesn't belong there.

✅ "The ancient text purports to be a lost gospel."

This works perfectly, because whether the text genuinely is a lost gospel is exactly what's in question.

So the word is always pointing at a gap — the gap between what something claims about itself and what the truth might actually be.

These two words are close, but not identical.

"Claim" is typically used for a person actively asserting something with words:

"He claims he was home all night."

"Purport" is more about appearance and presentation — what something seems or pretends to be, whether or not anyone is literally speaking:

"The signature purports to be hers."

A forged signature can't speak, but it presents itself as genuine. That's purporting. Also, "purport" is more formal and tends to carry a slightly stronger shade of skepticism than "claim."

"Purport" is a formal word. You'll encounter it most often in:

  • Legal and court language ("the contract purports to waive all rights")
  • Journalism and investigative writing ("the leaked emails purport to show corruption")
  • Academic and scholarly writing ("the study purports to demonstrate a causal link")

You wouldn't typically use it in casual conversation — you'd sound overly stiff. But in formal writing, it's precise and powerful.
A Quick Summary to Lock It In

"Purport" = to present or claim to be something, with an implied "but I'm not so sure that's true."

It lives in the space between a thing's claim about itself and the unverified reality. Every time you see or use this word, the silent question hanging in the air is: Is it really what it says it is? That question is the heartbeat of the word.
12839:
"Purported" means claimed to be something, but not proven, and often doubted. When you put the word "purported" in front of something, you are saying: "Someone has said this is true, but I am not confirming it — and I may even be skeptical about it."

It is a word that carries a quiet warning: don't take this at face value.

Imagine someone hands you a letter and says, "This is a letter from the President." You haven't verified it. You don't know if it's real. You might even suspect it's fake. So instead of saying "Here is a letter from the President" (which would mean you believe it), you say: "Here is a purported letter from the President."

That one word — purported — tells the listener three things at once:

  1. Someone is making a claim.
  2. The claim has not been proven.
  3. You, the speaker, are keeping your distance from that claim. You are not vouching for it.

This is the most important thing to understand: "purported" almost always carries a shade of doubt or suspicion. It's not a neutral word. When a writer or speaker uses it, they are gently signaling to you, the reader, that you should not simply accept the claim as fact.

For example, if a news article says "the purported mastermind of the robbery was arrested," the journalist is saying: "Police or others claim this person is the mastermind — but this has not been proven in court, and we are not confirming it ourselves." The word protects the journalist from stating something as fact that may turn out to be wrong.
Who makes the claim vs. who uses the word

Here is a subtle but important point. The person using the word "purported" is usually not the one making the original claim. They are reporting someone else's claim while quietly distancing themselves from it.

Think of it this way: the claim belongs to someone else. "Purported" is how you hold it at arm's length, pass it to your audience, and say, "Someone said this — make of it what you will."

"The police found the purported murder weapon."
Someone claims this is the murder weapon. It has not been confirmed by a court or lab. The word "purported" tells you: don't treat this as established fact yet.

"He met with the purported leader of the organization."
Others say this person is the leader, but it's unverified — perhaps the organization is secret, or perhaps there's genuine uncertainty about who runs it.

"She bought a purported antique vase for thousands of dollars."
The seller claimed it was an antique. She believed it or at least paid for it as such. But "purported" hints that this claim may be false — perhaps it's a fake, and she was deceived.

"A man claiming to be a purported expert in nutrition gave a talk at the event."
Someone calls himself an expert, but the speaker using "purported" is signaling they are not convinced of his credentials.

"Purported" does not say the claim is definitely false. It leaves the door open. The antique might genuinely be an antique. The leader might truly be the leader. The murder weapon might really be the murder weapon. "Purported" simply says: we don't know yet, and we're not committing.

However, in practice, when writers use "purported," they often lean toward skepticism. If they fully believed the claim, they would just state it as fact. The very choice of this word is a signal that something feels unverified, untrustworthy, or at least unconfirmed.
How it compares to similar words

Three words behave similarly to "purported," and it helps to understand how they differ:

Alleged is the closest cousin. It also means "claimed but not proven." However, "alleged" is almost exclusively used in legal and criminal contexts — alleged thief, alleged fraud, alleged assault. "Purported" is broader and is used in everyday contexts too, not just legal ones.

Supposed is very similar to "purported" and often interchangeable. However, "supposed" can sometimes just mean "expected to" or "meant to" (as in "you're supposed to call me"), whereas "purported" almost always specifically means "claimed to be." "Purported" also tends to sound slightly more formal and carries a stronger sense of active skepticism.

So-called is the most dismissive of the group. When you say "the so-called expert," you are being openly sarcastic — you are clearly saying you don't believe the claim at all. "Purported" is more neutral and professional; it raises doubt without openly mocking.
Where you will most commonly see this word

You will find "purported" most often in journalism, legal writing, and formal reports. These are fields where accuracy matters enormously, and writers cannot afford to state unverified claims as facts. The word is their tool for reporting what someone else has claimed — honestly, carefully, and without personally endorsing it.

You might also see it in everyday speech when someone is being deliberately careful or cautious about a claim they've heard but don't fully trust.
If you ever need to recall what "purported" means, remember this: it means "claimed to be, but not proven — and probably viewed with some doubt."
12840:
To purse means to press your lips together tightly so that they form a small, puckered, rounded shape — almost like a tiny knot or a small "o" pulled inward. Think of how a drawstring bag closes when you pull the strings: the opening gathers, tightens, and puckers into a small, bunched circle. When you purse your lips, your mouth does exactly that.

This verb is almost always used with the word lips as its object. You will almost never see "purse" used as a verb without lips being involved.

Picture someone who has just tasted something unpleasant, or someone who is trying very hard not to say what they're thinking. Their lips press together, squeeze inward slightly, and form a tight little round shape — not quite a smile, not quite a frown, but a firm, compact expression. That is pursed lips.

This is where the word gets really interesting and useful. People purse their lips for several reasons, and a good writer or speaker uses this word deliberately because it carries emotional meaning:

Disapproval or annoyance — This is the most common one. When someone hears something they don't like or disagrees strongly, they may purse their lips instead of speaking. It signals silent judgment.

Holding something back — A person might purse their lips to stop themselves from laughing, from crying, or from saying something they shouldn't. The tightness of the lips physically holds things in.

Concentration or deep thought — Sometimes people purse their lips when they are thinking hard about something, especially when working through a difficult decision.

Skepticism or doubt — When someone is not convinced by what you've just said, pursed lips can signal "I'm not sure I believe you."

"Purse" is a transitive verb, meaning it needs an object — and that object is almost always lips. The structure is simple:

  • Subject + pursed + his/her/their lips

It's most often used in the past tense because writers use it to describe a character's reaction in a moment:

"She pursed her lips."

You can also use it as a present participle to show an ongoing action or to modify a noun:

"He sat there, pursing his lips thoughtfully."
"She gave him a pursing-lips kind of look." (informal, rare)

Here are clear, natural examples so you can see the word in action:

  • "The teacher pursed her lips when she saw the messy classroom." — She was displeased but didn't say anything.
  • "He pursed his lips, staring at the math problem for a long time." — Deep concentration.
  • "She pursed her lips to keep from laughing out loud." — Holding back laughter.
  • "My mother pursed her lips when I told her my plan." — Quiet disapproval.
  • "The doctor pursed her lips and nodded slowly before delivering the news." — Thoughtfulness mixed with seriousness.

When you see "pursed lips" in a book or hear someone describe an expression this way, know that it is rarely neutral. Pursed lips almost always mean that a person is feeling something strongly but choosing not to say it outright — whether that's annoyance, doubt, amusement, or deep thought. It is the face of someone holding something inside.

That's the full picture of "purse" as a verb: a tight, puckered pressing of the lips together, loaded with quiet but unmistakable emotion.
12841:
"Pursuant" as an adjective lives almost entirely inside one phrase: "pursuant to." Mastering that two-word phrase is all you need.

"Pursuant to" means in accordance with, following from, or as required or authorized by something. It tells you that an action, decision, or situation exists because of — and in direct obedience or response to — whatever comes right after those two words. That "whatever" is almost always a rule, law, contract, order, or request.

The simplest way to see it in action:

"Pursuant to the contract, payment is due on Friday."

This means: "In accordance with what the contract says — following its terms — payment is due on Friday." The contract is the source. The payment deadline obeys and flows directly from it.

Another example:

"Pursuant to your request, I have attached the report."

This means: "Following your request, and in direct response to it, here is the report." Your request is the source. The attached report is the action that follows from it.

While the core idea stays consistent, "pursuant to" carries slightly different flavors depending on context.

The most common use is "in accordance with / as required by" — when a law, regulation, or agreement is the governing source: "Pursuant to federal law, all employees must be paid minimum wage." Here, the law is the authority, and the requirement follows directly from it.

The second use is "following / in response to" — when an action is a direct follow-up to a request or prior event: "Pursuant to our last conversation, I have drafted the proposal." The conversation prompted the action; the proposal is its direct result.

A third, older and rarer use means "in pursuit of / for the purpose of achieving" something: "measures taken pursuant to peace." This means measures taken with the aim of bringing about peace. You'll rarely encounter this version in modern writing, but it's worth knowing.
How to recognize it and where you'll see it

"Pursuant" is a formal word. You will almost never hear it in everyday conversation. It lives in legal documents, official letters, government notices, business contracts, and formal correspondence. When writing casually, people replace it with simpler alternatives: "as required by the contract," "following your request," "in line with the law." But in formal or legal writing, "pursuant to" is the standard go-to phrase, and you will see it constantly.

Technically, "pursuant" is an adjective because it modifies the subject of a sentence by describing its relationship to something else. In "actions taken pursuant to the agreement," the word "pursuant" describes the actions — it tells you their nature: that they follow from and comply with the agreement. However, in practice, the full phrase "pursuant to" behaves like a preposition — it connects what comes before it (an action or fact) to what comes after it (its source or basis). Don't lose sleep over the grammar label. What matters is how it functions: it links something to the rule, authority, or event that caused or governs it.

Because "pursuant" and "pursuit" share the same root, people sometimes mix up "pursuant to" with "in pursuit of." These are not the same thing in modern usage.

"He acted pursuant to the law" means he acted in accordance with the law — he followed it.

"He acted in pursuit of the criminal" means he chased the criminal.

In modern English, "pursuant to" almost never means physically chasing or hunting. It means following from, obeying, or acting in line with something.

Any time you see "pursuant to" in a sentence, try swapping it with "in accordance with" or "as required by." If the sentence still makes sense, you've read the word correctly. In the vast majority of cases, this substitution will work perfectly, and you'll know exactly what the sentence means.
12842:
Pursue means to go after something — with intention, effort, and persistence over time.

The "going after" can be physical (chasing someone down a street) or it can be mental and emotional (spending years working toward a dream). Both are correct uses of the same word.

The three invisible qualities hidden inside "pursue" are:

  • Direction — you are moving toward something specific
  • Effort — it requires active doing, not passive waiting
  • Continuity — it happens over a period of time, not in a single instant

1. To physically chase or follow someone or something

This is the most literal, visual sense of the word. One thing moves, and you go after it.

The police pursued the suspect through the alley.
The lioness pursued the zebra across the open field.

Here, "pursue" and "chase" are nearly identical. The difference is subtle: "chase" feels more urgent and short-lived, while "pursue" can suggest a longer, more determined effort.

2. To work toward a goal, dream, or ambition

This is the most common and important meaning you will encounter. When someone "pursues" a dream, a career, or success, it means they are consistently putting in effort over time to reach it.

She pursued her dream of becoming a surgeon for over a decade.
He left his home country to pursue a better life.
They pursued excellence in everything they did.

Notice that this meaning lives entirely in the mind and in action — there is no physical chasing involved. Yet it perfectly fits the word because the core idea is still: going after something intentionally, with effort, over time.

3. To continue doing an activity, study, or interest

When you "pursue" a subject or activity, you are actively engaging in it on an ongoing basis — it is something you keep coming back to and developing.

After retiring, he pursued painting as a serious hobby.
The university encouraged her to pursue research in climate science.
She pursued her studies even while working two jobs.

The key here is the word ongoing. You don't "pursue" something you did once. You pursue something you dedicate time and energy to, repeatedly.

4. To keep investigating, discussing, or following up on something

In conversations, meetings, or professional life, "pursue" means to take something further — to not let it drop, but to keep pushing on it.

The detective pursued every lead until she found the truth.
The journalist pursued the story for six months before publishing.
I don't want to pursue this argument any further tonight.
The company decided not to pursue the matter in court.

Here, "pursue" is about sustained attention — you are actively following something through, rather than leaving it unfinished.

5. To seek someone's romantic attention

When a person "pursues" another person romantically, it means they are making persistent, deliberate efforts to attract or win that person's affection.

He had been pursuing her for months before she agreed to a date.
She wasn't interested in being pursued by anyone at that point in her life.
The One Thread That Ties All Meanings Together

No matter which situation you use it in, pursue always carries the same DNA:

Something exists that you want → you move toward it → you keep at it → it takes time and effort.

Whether it is a thief running away, a lifelong dream, a research project, a romantic interest, or an unresolved conversation — the word "pursue" fits whenever that formula applies.

• It is not a one-time action. You don't "pursue" something you did once by accident. The word implies sustained, deliberate effort.
  • It is not passive. You cannot pursue something while sitting still and waiting. Pursuing requires you to actively move toward the thing.
  • It is not the same as "reach" or "achieve." Pursuing is the journey. You pursue a goal; you achieve it (or don't) later.
A Useful Way to Remember It

Think of the word pursue as carrying a built-in image: a person walking steadily forward, eyes fixed on something in the distance, not giving up.

That image — steady, intentional, forward-moving, not stopping — is what the word means in every context it is used.

• pursue a dream / goal / passion / ambition
  • pursue a career / education / degree
  • pursue a matter / case / lead / story
  • pursue someone (romantically or in a chase)
  • pursue happiness / freedom / truth
  • actively / aggressively / relentlessly / vigorously pursue

The word pairs naturally with things that are worth going after and that require sustained effort to reach.
12843:
Pursuit means actively going after something. Whether you are physically chasing someone, working hard to achieve a goal, or engaging in a regular activity you love — the word "pursuit" captures the idea of ongoing, directed effort toward something.

Think of it this way: pursuit is never passive. It always involves movement — physical or figurative — toward something.
Meaning 1: Physically Chasing Someone or Something

The most literal sense. When you run after someone to catch them, that is a pursuit.

"The police car raced through the streets in pursuit of the stolen vehicle."

"The cat leaped over the fence, and the dog followed in hot pursuit."

Notice the phrase "in pursuit of" — it simply means "in the act of chasing." "Hot pursuit" is a common expression meaning the chase is immediate and very close — the pursuer is right behind.

This meaning is common in news reports, crime stories, and action scenes. The chaser wants to catch something; the pursuit is the act of trying to do so.
Meaning 2: Trying to Achieve or Obtain Something (Most Common Meaning)

This is the most widely used sense of the word, and it is metaphorical — not physical chasing, but the sustained effort of working toward a goal or an ideal.

"She spent years in the pursuit of knowledge."

"He sacrificed everything in his pursuit of success."

"The pursuit of happiness is a fundamental human desire."

Here, "pursuit" suggests that the thing you want is not yet fully in your hands — you are still striving toward it. It also implies that the process of going after it takes real, ongoing effort.

A very important detail: pursuit here often implies that reaching the goal is not guaranteed. It is the journey of trying, not the moment of arrival. You can spend a lifetime in the pursuit of wisdom without ever feeling you've fully achieved it — and that's the point. The word respects both the effort and the difficulty.

Common patterns you will see:

  • the pursuit of + [abstract noun] → pursuit of truth, pursuit of excellence, pursuit of power, pursuit of justice, pursuit of peace, pursuit of wealth

This is the sense used in one of the most famous phrases in political history: "Life, Liberty, and the pursuit of Happiness" — from the American Declaration of Independence. Notice it doesn't say happiness itself is guaranteed, only the pursuit of it.
Meaning 3: A Regular Activity or Hobby

"Pursuit" can also refer to an activity that someone regularly engages in — a hobby, occupation, or pastime. In this sense, it is a slightly formal word for "something you do."

"Reading, painting, and hiking are her favourite pursuits."

"He gave up his outdoor pursuits after the injury."

"Academic pursuits took up most of his time."

This meaning is quite neutral in tone — it simply names what someone spends their time doing. The word carries a subtle implication that the activity requires some effort or engagement (not something mindless), but it doesn't have to be grand or noble. A person's pursuits are simply the activities that define how they spend their time and energy.
The Thread Connecting All Three Meanings

All three meanings share one thing: active, directed effort. Whether you are chasing a thief, chasing a dream, or regularly engaging in something you love — in every case, you are going toward something with energy and intention.

The word never applies to something passive or accidental. You don't stumble into a pursuit — you engage in one.

"Pursuit" is a moderately formal word. It fits naturally in writing, speeches, and thoughtful conversation. In casual speech, people might simply say "going after" or "chasing" something, but when they want to sound more considered or serious, they reach for pursuit.

It also carries a slightly dignified, even noble connotation, especially in Meaning 2. Saying someone is in the pursuit of justice sounds more weighty and sincere than just saying they are trying to get justice. The word respects the effort involved.

UseWhat it meansExample
  • Chasing physically → running after someone to catch them (in pursuit of the thief)
  • Working toward a goal → sustained effort to achieve something (pursuit of happiness/knowledge)
  • A regular activity → a hobby or occupation (outdoor pursuits; academic pursuits)
Think of pursuit as the journey of going after — whether that is a person, a dream, or a passion. The word lives in the space between starting and arriving, and it honours the effort in between.
12844:
To purvey means to supply or provide something — but not in a casual, one-off way. It carries the sense of doing so regularly, professionally, or as an established role. Think of it as a more formal, deliberate kind of providing.

The simplest test: if someone purveys something, they are in the business of making it available to others, consistently and intentionally.

Sense 1 — To supply goods (especially food, drink, or provisions)

This is the oldest and most traditional meaning. It describes the act of sourcing and supplying goods — historically food and drink — to people, establishments, or institutions.

"The family has been purveying fine cheeses to restaurants in the city for over a century."

"The company purveys organic vegetables to schools and hospitals across the region."

Notice that in both examples, the supply is not random or accidental. There is an ongoing, professional relationship between the supplier and the recipient. The word implies a certain established presence in that role.

This is why you often see the related noun purveyor used in formal or high-end commercial contexts — "Purveyor of Fine Foods" — because it signals that someone is not just selling things occasionally, but is dedicated to that supply as their function.

Sense 2 — To spread or circulate ideas, information, content, or culture

In its extended modern use, purvey moves beyond physical goods. It can describe the act of putting out or spreading ideas, stories, information, entertainment, propaganda, or anything that is distributed to an audience.

"That channel has been purveying misinformation for years."

"She built her career purveying escapist romantic fiction to millions of readers."

"The regime used state television to purvey its ideology to the population."

Here, the word still carries the same core flavour — it is systematic, deliberate, and ongoing. You don't purvey something by accident. There is always an intentional, sustained effort behind it.
The Tone and Register of the Word

Purvey is a formal word. You would not hear it in casual conversation. Nobody says "I purveyed some snacks to my friends." In everyday speech, people say provide, supply, sell, or distribute.

You encounter purvey in:

  • Formal business or commercial writing ("purveying luxury goods to discerning clients")
  • Journalism or criticism ("a media outlet that purveys outrage for profit")
  • Literary or elevated prose ("he spent his life purveying half-truths")

When a writer chooses purvey over provide or supply, they are adding a subtle layer of meaning — suggesting that the act is deliberate, professional, and part of an established pattern, rather than something casual or accidental.
What Makes It Different from Simple Synonyms

You might wonder: why not just say supply or provide? Here is the key distinction:

  • Supply / provide are neutral and general. They say nothing about the nature of the relationship or the role of the person doing it.
  • Purvey implies that the person doing it is in a recognised or established capacity as a supplier or distributor. It suggests they are the dedicated source of something for others.

Similarly, compared to sell:

  • Sell focuses on the commercial transaction (money changes hands).
  • Purvey focuses on the role of being the one who makes something available — whether for profit or not.

When purvey is used in Sense 2 — spreading ideas or content — it very often carries a slightly critical or disapproving tone, particularly when the thing being purveyed is undesirable.

"They have long been purveying conspiracy theories to a vulnerable audience."
"The tabloid purveys gossip and scandal."

This is not a strict rule — purvey can be neutral or even positive — but be aware that when a writer uses it to describe the spreading of information or ideas, there is often a quiet suggestion that the thing being purveyed is not entirely respectable, or that the act of spreading it is somewhat cynical.

What it meansTo supply or provide something on a regular, deliberate, professional basis
Physical senseSupplying goods (especially food/drink) to customers or institutions
Abstract senseSpreading ideas, information, content, or culture to an audience
Key flavourFormal; implies an established, ongoing role as a supplier
Tone when abstractOften slightly critical or disapproving
One Sentence to Remember It By

To purvey is to be the consistent, deliberate source from which something flows to others — whether that something is bread, beliefs, or propaganda.

Master that idea and you will read purvey correctly in any context you ever encounter it.
12845:
Purview means the range, scope, or extent of what something — or someone — is responsible for, has authority over, or is legitimately concerned with.

Imagine an invisible circle drawn around a person, a department, an institution, or a law. Everything inside that circle is their purview — their territory to handle, decide on, or care about. Everything outside that circle is not their purview — it's not their place to touch.

It is a formal word. You won't hear it in casual conversation, but you'll encounter it frequently in professional, legal, academic, and governmental contexts.

1. Scope of authority or responsibility

This is the most common use. When something is "within someone's purview," it means it falls under their authority or is their responsibility to deal with. When something is "outside their purview," it means it simply isn't their job or their call to make.

  • A hospital's medical ethics board has the power to approve or reject experimental treatments. Deciding the hospital's marketing budget is not within their purview — that belongs to management.
  • The fire department's purview is fire safety and emergency rescue. Investigating a theft is the police's purview, not theirs.
  • A school principal's purview includes discipline, curriculum, and staff — but rewriting the national education policy is well beyond their purview.

Notice the pattern: purview defines the boundary of legitimate involvement. It tells you where your authority starts and where it ends.

2. Range of awareness or understanding

Purview can also describe the limits of what someone is aware of, exposed to, or capable of perceiving — not because of a rule, but because of their position, knowledge, or experience.

  • For most people living in the 1800s, events happening on the other side of the world never entered their purview — they simply had no way of knowing.
  • The intricacies of quantum physics fall outside the purview of most non-scientists — not because they're forbidden from it, but because it lies beyond their exposure and understanding.

Here, purview isn't about authority — it's about the limits of someone's world or awareness.

3. The legal sense

In law, the purview of a statute (a written law) refers to what that law actually covers and intends to regulate. If something falls within the purview of a law, the law applies to it. If it falls outside, the law doesn't govern it.

  • A consumer protection law might have a purview that covers only individual buyers, not large corporations buying from other corporations.
  • A court may rule that a certain type of dispute falls outside the purview of a particular regulation, meaning that regulation simply doesn't apply to it.
The Phrases You'll Always See It In

Purview almost always appears with one of these constructions:

"Within the purview of" — it belongs to, it is covered by, it is their responsibility.

Reviewing employee performance is within the purview of the HR department.

"Outside/beyond the purview of" — it doesn't belong to them, it's not their territory.

Personal lifestyle choices are generally outside the purview of an employer.

"Under the purview of" — subject to the authority or supervision of.

Food safety standards fall under the purview of the national health authority.

"The purview of [something]" — the defined scope belonging to that thing.

The committee expanded its purview to include cybersecurity issues.
How Purview Differs From Similar Words

These three words are close neighbors, and understanding the difference will sharpen your use of purview:

Purview vs. Scope
Scope is a more neutral word that simply means the range or extent of something — a project's scope, the scope of a study. Purview carries the extra sense of legitimate claim or authority. It's not just what something covers, but what something has the right to cover or act on.

Purview vs. Jurisdiction
Jurisdiction specifically refers to the official legal authority of courts, governments, or law enforcement. Purview is broader and less formal in the sense that it can apply to any person, role, subject, or organization — not just official legal bodies.

Purview vs. Domain
Domain refers to a general area of knowledge or activity (the domain of science, the domain of art). Purview emphasizes the limits and boundaries of that area more explicitly, and it more strongly implies authority or responsibility within those limits.

Purview is the defined territory — whether of authority, responsibility, or awareness — that belongs to a person, institution, law, or subject: what falls inside it is their business to handle or know; what falls outside it is not.
12846:
Pusillanimity is the quality of being weak-spirited, cowardly, and timid — especially when a situation calls for courage, decisiveness, or standing up for what is right. A person who displays pusillanimity tends to shrink, cave, or back down not because the situation is truly overwhelming, but because they lack the inner strength and moral backbone to face it.

Think of it as a smallness of spirit. The word doesn't just mean being afraid. It means being so dominated by fear, self-preservation, or a desire to avoid discomfort that you fail to do what you know is right or necessary.
What Makes It Different From Ordinary Cowardice?

"Cowardice" and "pusillanimity" are close cousins, but pusillanimity is more specific and, in many ways, more damning.

Cowardice is primarily about fear — a soldier running from battle, for instance. It's reactive. Something scary happens, and the person flees.

Pusillanimity, on the other hand, is about a fundamental weakness of character. It's less about a single panicked reaction and more about a persistent, ingrained pattern of avoiding anything difficult, uncomfortable, or risky — even when the stakes are moral rather than physical. It implies a kind of pettiness and smallness alongside the fear.

A coward might be forgiven for panicking in a terrifying moment. A pusillanimous person has no such excuse — they are simply too weak-willed and self-concerned to act with integrity.

When someone accuses another person of pusillanimity, the accusation carries a particular flavor. It suggests that the person:

  • Knows the right thing to do, but refuses to do it out of fear or self-interest.
  • Caves under pressure easily, even when they shouldn't.
  • Avoids taking clear stands, preferring vague, non-committal positions to protect themselves.
  • Prioritizes their own comfort or safety over duty, principle, or the wellbeing of others.

It is a word that belongs to the world of moral judgment. You wouldn't use it to describe a child afraid of the dark. You would use it to describe an adult who, fully knowing what is right, chooses the path of least resistance instead.

Example 1 — The Silent Witness
A manager watches a senior colleague bully and humiliate a junior employee repeatedly. The manager knows it's wrong. They have the authority to stop it. But they say nothing, because confronting the senior colleague might create tension, put their own career at risk, or simply make their working life uncomfortable. That silence, that refusal to act despite knowing better — that is pusillanimity.

Example 2 — The Spineless Leader
A politician privately believes a certain policy is harmful and unjust. When the time comes to vote, they vote in favor of it anyway, because voting against it might cost them popularity, party support, or re-election. They have sacrificed their principles at the altar of self-preservation. This is a textbook case of pusillanimity.

Example 3 — The Hollow Friend
Your friend is being treated unfairly and asks you to speak up on their behalf to someone in power. You know they are right. You agree with them completely. But you stay quiet because you don't want to rock the boat or invite any criticism toward yourself. You later offer your friend private sympathy but public silence. That is pusillanimity.

In all three cases, notice the common thread: the person knows what courage demands of them, and they deliberately choose the weaker path.

To sharpen the definition further, it helps to know what this word does not mean.

  • It is not the same as introversion or shyness. Being quiet or reserved by nature is not pusillanimity. Pusillanimity is specifically about moral and personal courage, not personality type.
  • It is not the same as reasonable caution. Choosing not to pick a fight you cannot possibly win is wisdom, not pusillanimity. The word implies a failure that could and should have been avoided.
  • It is not always about physical fear. In fact, pusillanimity most often shows up in moral, social, or professional situations — places where physical danger is not involved at all, but where integrity is tested.
  • It is not the same as humility. A humble person defers to others because they genuinely respect them. A pusillanimous person defers because they lack the courage to do otherwise.

Pusillanimity is not a casual insult. It is a serious moral charge. When great thinkers, writers, or leaders have used this word across history, they have used it to describe one of the most disappointing things a person can be — not evil, not stupid, but small. Unwilling to rise to the occasion when it matters.

There is something almost sadder about pusillanimity than about outright villainy. The villain at least acts. The pusillanimous person simply... doesn't. They see, they understand, and they shrink.

If you had to capture the entire meaning of pusillanimity in one sentence, it would be this:

Pusillanimity is the quality of being so weak in spirit and so driven by self-preservation that you consistently fail to act with the courage, decisiveness, and integrity that the moment demands of you.
12847:
Pusillanimous means showing a shameful lack of courage or willpower — being so weak in character that you avoid anything difficult, risky, or confrontational, even when the situation genuinely calls for bravery or decisiveness.

In plain terms: a pusillanimous person is a coward — but not just in the physical sense. They are a coward in spirit.
What Makes It Different From Simply Being "Scared"

This is the most important thing to understand. Everyone feels fear. Fear is normal and human. A person can be terrified and still act bravely. That is not pusillanimous.

Pusillanimous describes someone who surrenders to their fear or weakness in a way that is morally contemptible — especially when others are depending on them, or when something important is at stake. It's about a failure of character, not just a feeling.

Think of it this way: a soldier who is scared but still charges forward is brave. A soldier who is scared, sees that people need help, and slinks away anyway — that is pusillanimous.
The Moral Sting in the Word

This word carries a strong negative judgment. When you call someone or something pusillanimous, you are not just describing them — you are disapproving of them, even looking down on them. It implies a smallness and pettiness of spirit.

It can describe:

  • A person who consistently avoids taking a stand or facing hard things
  • A decision or action that is half-hearted, weak, or disgracefully timid
  • A response that dodges difficulty when boldness was needed

Pusillanimous is a fairly formal, literary word. You'll see it more in writing than in everyday conversation. It's especially common in:

  • Political commentary — criticizing leaders who fail to act decisively or take a moral stand
  • Literary or historical writing — describing characters or figures who lack backbone
  • Formal criticism — calling out an organization, institution, or policy for being spineless

These examples will show you exactly how the word works in context:

  1. "The senator's pusillanimous refusal to vote on the bill — out of fear of upsetting donors — outraged his constituents." (He had a moral duty to act, but cowardice won.)
  2. "She gave a pusillanimous apology that admitted nothing and satisfied no one." (The apology was so weak and evasive it was almost an insult in itself.)
  3. "History will not be kind to those who offered a pusillanimous response when decisive action was needed." (A moment called for courage; they delivered weakness.)
  4. "Stop being so pusillanimous and just tell your boss what you actually think." (Said in frustration to someone who keeps backing down from honest confrontation.)
How It Compares to Similar Words

Understanding a word fully means knowing where it sits among its neighbors:

  • Timid — mild. A timid person is shy and hesitant by nature. No strong blame is attached. A child can be timid; that's okay.
  • Cowardly — strong. Very close to pusillanimous, but cowardly can describe a single act ("a cowardly attack from behind"). Pusillanimous tends to describe a pattern or quality of character — it feels more like a deep-seated failing than a single bad moment.
  • Faint-hearted — moderate. Similar idea, but softer and less condemnatory than pusillanimous.
  • Spineless — strong and vivid. Very close in meaning. Spineless is more casual and punchy; pusillanimous is more formal and carries an air of measured contempt.
  • Gutless — very casual, blunt, and angry. Pusillanimous is the word you use when you want to sound more considered and authoritative in your condemnation.

Pusillanimous is the most formal and arguably the most cutting of these, because it sounds deliberate and considered — like a verdict, not just an insult flung in the heat of the moment.
The Single Most Important Thing to Remember

Pusillanimous = weak and cowardly in a way that is morally shameful — not just scared, but too spineless to do what is right or necessary when it truly matters.

If you ever use this word or read it, that judgment — that quiet but sharp contempt for weakness of character — is always present in it.
12848: Before diving in, let's quickly clarify what a phrasal verb is. A phrasal verb is a verb combined with one or more small words (like off, up, out, in) that together create a new meaning — a meaning that is often completely different from the original verb. For example, "put" means to place something somewhere, but "put off" means something entirely different. This is what makes phrasal verbs tricky, and why you need to learn them as whole units.
"Put Off" — The Core Idea

There is one simple image that connects almost all meanings of "put off": the idea of something being pushed away — either in time, or in feeling. Keep this image in mind, and the meanings will make much more sense.
Meaning 1: To Postpone (Delay Something to a Later Time)

This is the most common meaning.

When you put something off, you decide not to do it now and move it to a later time. You are essentially "pushing it away" into the future.

Examples:

  • "I have a dentist appointment tomorrow, but I'm going to put it off until next month." (I'll reschedule it for later.)
  • "She keeps putting off her homework and then panics at night."
  • "Don't put off important decisions — they don't disappear on their own."
  • "The match was put off because of heavy rain." (It was postponed.)

In everyday life, this meaning shows up constantly. Whenever people delay doing something unpleasant or difficult, they are "putting it off." Paying bills, having a hard conversation, going to the doctor — these are all things people commonly put off.

A famous saying you should know:

"Never put off till tomorrow what you can do today."

This is one of the most well-known English proverbs, and now you understand it perfectly.
Meaning 2: To Make Someone Lose Interest, Enthusiasm, or Appetite

This is the second most important meaning, and it is very different from the first. Here, "put off" means to repel, discourage, or disgust someone — to make them not want something anymore.

Think of it like pushing someone away from something emotionally.

Examples:

  • "The terrible smell put me off my food." (I lost my appetite because of it.)
  • "His rude behavior put her off immediately." (She lost interest in him.)
  • "The long waiting lines put me off visiting the museum."
  • "I was going to apply for the job, but the low salary put me off."

Notice that this meaning can work in two slightly different ways:

a) Someone is put off by something (a person, a thing, or a situation causes the feeling):

  • "I was put off by his arrogance."

b) Something puts you off doing something (you stop wanting to do a specific thing):

  • "The accident put me off driving for months."
  • "That bad experience put me off eating seafood."

Both are natural and very common.
Meaning 3: To Cause Someone to Dislike Something (Often Permanently)

This is closely related to Meaning 2, but the result is more lasting. Here, "put off" means something has caused you to develop a long-term dislike or aversion to something.

Examples:

  • "I had food poisoning from that restaurant, and it completely put me off spicy food."
  • "His dishonesty put her off relationships for a long time."
  • "One bad teacher can put a child off reading for years."

The key difference from Meaning 2 is the depth and duration. In Meaning 2, you just lose interest in a moment. In Meaning 3, the dislike tends to stick around.
Meaning 4: To Distract Someone and Break Their Concentration

Here, "put off" means to break someone's focus or disrupt their performance. You are "pushing away" their ability to concentrate.

Examples:

  • "Stop humming! You're putting me off." (You are distracting me.)
  • "The loud crowd put the tennis player off, and she made several mistakes."
  • "Don't put me off while I'm counting — I'll have to start again."

This meaning is very common in British English and appears often in sports contexts. It's about something external interrupting your mental focus.
Meaning 5: To Avoid Someone or Delay Dealing With Them (Using Excuses)

In this meaning, you "put someone off" by giving them excuses, delays, or vague promises instead of dealing with them directly. You are pushing the person away rather than dealing with the matter.

Examples:

  • "I've been trying to speak to the manager for a week, but they keep putting me off."
  • "She didn't want to say no, so she put him off by saying she was busy."
  • "Every time I asked for my money back, he put me off with excuses."

Notice that in this meaning, the object is always a person, not a thing.
Meaning 6: To Drop Someone Off a Vehicle (Uncommon but Real)

This is a less frequent meaning, but you may encounter it. It means to let someone get off a bus, train, or other vehicle — sometimes even against their will.

Examples:

  • "The conductor put the passenger off at the next stop because he had no ticket."
  • "The driver put us off at the wrong terminal."

You are unlikely to use this meaning in everyday conversation, but it's good to recognize it.
The Grammar of "Put Off" — Very Important

"Put off" is what's called a separable phrasal verb. This means the object (the thing or person you're talking about) can go in two positions:

Position A — Object after "off":

  • "I put off the meeting."
  • "She put off her appointment."

Position B — Object between "put" and "off":

  • "I put the meeting off."
  • "She put her appointment off."

Both are equally correct. However, there is one strict rule you must never break:

If the object is a pronoun (it, him, her, them, me, us), it MUST go in the middle. It can NEVER go after "off."

✅ "I put it off." (correct)
❌ "I put off it." (wrong — never say this)

✅ "His behavior put me off." (correct)
❌ "His behavior put off me." (wrong)

This rule applies to all separable phrasal verbs in English, so remembering it here will help you across the board.
How to Tell Which Meaning Is Being Used

Since "put off" has multiple meanings, context is your best tool. Here are some quick clues:

  • If the object is a task, event, or plan → likely Meaning 1 (postpone).
  • If someone mentions feeling disgusted, repelled, or losing interest → Meaning 2 or 3.
  • If someone is talking about focus, concentration, or performance → Meaning 4.
  • If someone is being avoided or fobbed off with excuses → Meaning 5.
Common Collocations (Words Frequently Used Together With "Put Off")

Some things are very commonly "put off" in English. Knowing these combinations helps you sound natural:

  • Put off a meeting / appointment / trip / decision / task / payment / deadline / conversation / wedding
  • Put off doing homework / going to the doctor / making a call / starting a project
  • Be put off by someone's attitude / a smell / the price / bad reviews / a rude comment
Quick Summary of All Meanings

1. Postpone → "I put off the meeting."
2. Discourage / repel → "The price put me off buying it."
3. Cause lasting dislike → "That incident put me off flying forever."
4. Distract / break concentration → "Stop talking — you're putting me off."
5. Avoid someone with excuses → "They kept putting me off."
6. Drop off a vehicle → "The driver put them off at the station." (rare)
A Final Note on Tone

"Put off" in all its meanings carries a slightly negative or reluctant feeling. Postponing something usually implies you don't want to deal with it. Being put off means something has disappointed or repelled you. Being put off by someone means they failed to handle you properly. This underlying negativity is the emotional thread that runs through every meaning, and recognizing it will help you use "put off" with exactly the right nuance every time.
12849:
To put one's finger on something means to identify or pinpoint exactly what something is — especially when that thing is unclear, vague, or hard to define.

Think of it this way: imagine a map spread out on a table, and someone asks, "Where is the problem?" Instead of waving your hand over a wide area, you press your finger on the exact spot. That physical act of pointing to the precise location is the image behind this idiom. Mentally, it means the same thing — finding the exact thing, not just a general idea of it.
The Two Ways It Is Used

This idiom is used in two situations, and understanding both is important.

1. When you successfully identify something

Here, you managed to figure out the exact thing — a problem, a cause, a difference, or a feeling.

"After hours of thinking, she finally put her finger on what was wrong with the plan."
(= She finally identified the exact problem.)

"The doctor put his finger on the cause of the patient's illness immediately."
(= The doctor identified the exact cause.)

2. When you are struggling to identify something (the more common use)

Here, you sense that something is there — a feeling, a problem, something odd — but you cannot name or define it precisely. This form almost always uses the word "can't" or "couldn't."

"Something about his story feels wrong, but I can't put my finger on it."
(= I sense something is off, but I can't identify exactly what it is.)

"There's something different about this painting today. I just can't put my finger on it."
(= I notice a difference, but I can't pinpoint what it is.)

This second use is extremely common in everyday English, and if you only remember one form, remember: "I can't put my finger on it."
What Kind of Things Is It Used For?

This idiom is almost always used for abstract things — things you cannot physically touch. These include:

  • A problem ("I can't put my finger on the problem.")
  • A feeling ("I can't put my finger on this strange feeling.")
  • A reason ("She couldn't put her finger on why she felt so uncomfortable.")
  • A difference ("Something changed between them. I can't put my finger on what.")
  • A mistake or error ("He read the report twice but couldn't put his finger on the mistake.")

You would not normally use this idiom for something you can literally point at physically. It's for things that live in the mind — feelings, ideas, causes, reasons.

The idiom follows this pattern:

Subject + put/can't put + possessive + finger + on + it/something/what/why/the [noun]

Here are the variations:

  • I can't put my finger on it. (most common)
  • She finally put her finger on the problem.
  • They couldn't put their fingers on what was different.
  • Can you put your finger on why this doesn't feel right?
  • He put his finger on the exact moment things went wrong.

Notice how the possessive changes depending on who is doing it: my, your, his, her, their, our.

What makes this idiom so useful is that it captures a very specific human experience — that frustrating feeling when you know something is there, you can almost feel it, but you just cannot name it. Like when a word is on the tip of your tongue, or when a movie looks familiar but you can't remember where you've seen it. That experience of almost-but-not-quite knowing is exactly what "I can't put my finger on it" expresses — and no single ordinary word captures it quite as well.
Where Did This Idiom Come From?

The idiom comes from the literal, physical action of pressing your finger on an exact spot — like pointing to a precise location on a map, or touching a specific line in a book. When you put your finger on something physically, you are being exact and precise. Over time, this idea of physical precision was borrowed into mental and intellectual situations — "putting your finger on" an idea, a problem, or a feeling means finding the exact mental equivalent of that pinpoint.

Knowing similar expressions will help you understand this one more deeply.

  • "Figure out" — more general; means to solve or understand something. "I figured out the problem" just means you solved it. "Put my finger on the problem" specifically means you identified and named the exact issue with precision.
  • "Pin down" — very similar; means to identify or define something that keeps escaping definition. "I can't pin down what's bothering me." The difference is subtle — pin down often implies something that is moving or changing, while put your finger on implies something that is vague or elusive.
  • "Zero in on" — means to focus your attention toward something and identify it. It has more of a sense of actively searching and narrowing down. "The detective zeroed in on the suspect."
  • "Nail it down" — means to define or confirm something precisely. Slightly more forceful in tone than put your finger on.

Among all of these, "I can't put my finger on it" is the most commonly used in natural, everyday conversation.

SituationExample

At work: "There's something off about this report, but I can't put my finger on what it is."

In a relationship: "He felt something had changed between them, but he couldn't put his finger on it."

About food: "This dish tastes strange. I can't put my finger on which ingredient is wrong."

About a person: "She reminds me of someone. I just can't put my finger on who."

In medicine: "After running several tests, the doctor finally put her finger on the diagnosis."

About yourself: "I've been feeling uneasy all day, but I can't put my finger on why."

If you want to remember this idiom for life, hold onto this image:

Someone pointing with one finger at the exact spot on a map — not waving at the whole map, not pointing to a general area, but pressing one finger on the precise location.

That precision — that "exact-ness" — is the heart of this idiom. Whether you found it ("I put my finger on it") or you're still searching ("I can't put my finger on it") — the idiom is always about the quest for pinpoint identification.
12850:
Imagine a child who keeps asking their parent to stay up past bedtime. Night after night, the parent gives in. But one night, the parent says firmly: "No. Bedtime is 9 PM and that is final. I am not changing my mind." That parent has put their foot down.

"Put one's foot down" means to make a firm, final decision and refuse to change it, no matter what. It is about asserting authority or taking a strong stand on something.

This idiom has two distinct meanings. You must know both.

Meaning 1: To be firm and refuse to allow something (the main, most common meaning)

This is what most people mean when they use this idiom. When someone puts their foot down, they:

  • Take a clear, strong position on something
  • Refuse to negotiate, compromise, or back down
  • Use their authority to stop or demand something

The person is essentially saying: "This is where I draw the line. I will not tolerate or accept this any further."

Examples:

  • "My teenage son wanted to skip school every Friday, but I put my foot down and told him absolutely not."
  • "The employees kept arriving late every day, so the manager finally put her foot down and warned that it would affect their salaries."
  • "She had been letting her friend borrow money for months without getting it back. She finally put her foot down and said no more."
  • "The government put its foot down on illegal dumping and started handing out heavy fines."

Notice that in all these examples, the person using the idiom has authority over the situation — they are a parent, a manager, a friend with a boundary, or a government. Putting your foot down means you have the power to enforce what you are saying.

Meaning 2: To press the accelerator and speed up (used in British English, especially)

This is a much more literal and physical meaning. In driving, your foot presses down on the accelerator pedal to make the car go faster. So "put your foot down" simply means to accelerate or drive faster.

Examples:

  • "We're going to be late — put your foot down!"
  • "As soon as we got onto the highway, he put his foot down and the car shot forward."

This meaning is more common in British English than American English. In American English, people are more likely to say "step on it" or "floor it" for the same idea.

In everyday conversation, unless someone is clearly talking about driving, assume they are using Meaning 1.
Where Does This Idiom Come From?

The origin of Meaning 1 is rooted in body language and human behavior. When someone is angry, serious, or commanding, they often stamp or plant their foot firmly on the ground. Think of a general standing firm on a battlefield, or a person literally stomping their foot to show they will not budge. The foot is on the ground — solid, heavy, immovable. That image of firmness and refusal to move is where the idiom gets its meaning.

For Meaning 2, the origin is straightforward — it literally describes the physical act of pressing your foot onto the car's accelerator pedal.
The Feeling and Tone Behind the Idiom

When someone "puts their foot down," there is almost always a story leading up to it. This idiom implies that the person has been patient for a while, but has now reached their limit. There is a sense of:

  • Enough is enough.
  • I have been lenient, but no more.
  • My decision is made and it is non-negotiable.

This is why you'll often hear it used with words like "finally" or "eventually":

  • "She finally put her foot down."
  • "He eventually put his foot down."

These words confirm that patience ran out before the person acted firmly.

You'll hear this idiom in everyday, informal conversations — between friends, family members, and colleagues. It is not overly formal or overly casual. It sits comfortably in the middle, which means it works in most situations — at home, at work, and in general discussions.

It is used when talking about:

  • Parenting — "She put her foot down about screen time."
  • Relationships — "He put his foot down about going to the party."
  • Workplace situations — "The boss put her foot down about the dress code."
  • Personal boundaries — "I put my foot down and stopped letting people take advantage of me."
  • Politics and authority — "The prime minister put his foot down on immigration reform."

The idiom works with many subjects. Here are the patterns:

  • I / You / He / She / We / They + put(s) their foot down
  • "She put her foot down."
  • "He needs to put his foot down."
  • "I finally put my foot down."
  • "The school put its foot down on bullying."

Notice that the possessive (my, his, her, its, their) changes depending on the subject, but the idiom itself stays the same.

Because the word "foot" is in this idiom, beginners sometimes confuse it with other foot-related idioms. Here is a quick heads-up:

  • "Put your foot in your mouth" — This means to say something embarrassing or socially awkward by accident. It has nothing to do with authority or firmness. (Example: "I put my foot in my mouth when I forgot his wife's name.")
  • "Get off on the wrong foot" — This means to start a relationship or situation badly. (Example: "We got off on the wrong foot when I arrived late to our first meeting.")
  • "Have one foot in the grave" — This means to be very old or very ill, close to death.

None of these mean "put one's foot down." Keep them separate in your mind.

Main meaningTo firmly refuse something or insist that a decision is final
Second meaningTo press the accelerator and drive faster (mostly British English)
ToneFirm, authoritative, decisive
Implied backstoryThe person has tolerated something for too long and is now taking a stand
RegisterInformal to neutral — works in most everyday contexts
One Final Example to Cement It All

"For years, Marcus let his roommate leave dirty dishes in the sink without saying anything. He didn't want to cause trouble.
